body:
Why Arab accounts are important

From the early-medieval period, merchants and travellers connected the western coast of India with ports around the Arabian Sea and the Persian Gulf. Their writings sometimes described the rulers whose territories or spheres of influence were connected with these trading routes.

Such accounts help identify how the Rashtrakutas were known outside India. They also show that the history of an inland Deccan kingdom was connected with maritime trade.

Sulaiman and the name Balhara

An important Arab account is associated with the merchant and traveller Sulaiman, writing around 851 CE. His account describes a powerful Indian ruler called the Balhara and places him among the major rulers known to contemporary merchants.

The name Balhara is generally understood as an Arabic rendering of the royal title Vallabharaja, associated with the Rashtrakuta rulers. It should not be mistaken for the name of a separate dynasty or a different capital.

Sulaiman's account belongs to the period of Amoghavarsha I, whose reign is generally dated to approximately 814–878 CE. The relationship is chronological: Sulaiman wrote while Amoghavarsha I was ruling.

Sulaiman, 851 CE: Arab account mentioning the Balhara, a title associated with the Rashtrakuta king. The account is contemporary with Amoghavarsha I.

Al-Masudi and the western coastal connections

Another important Arabic writer, Al-Masudi, wrote in the early 10th century CE. His descriptions also refer to the Balhara and to commercial communities connected with the western Indian coast.

Arabic accounts describe favourable relations between some Rashtrakuta rulers and Muslim merchants. They also report that Muslim trading communities were permitted to maintain places of worship at certain coastal settlements. These statements describe conditions reported by particular writers; they should not be converted into a claim that every port had identical arrangements throughout the dynasty's history.

The political and economic relationship was straightforward. Merchants benefited from access to trading settlements and routes, while rulers and regional authorities could benefit from commercial activity, duties and connections with distant markets.

What connected the Deccan to overseas trade?

The principal overseas route was the Arabian Sea, linking western India with Arabia, the Persian Gulf and other parts of the Indian Ocean trading world. Goods moved between coastal markets and inland regions through land routes.

Some important places associated with these western connections were:

PlacePresent-day locationHistorical importance
SanjanValsad district, GujaratEarly-medieval port with links to overseas commerce.
SoparaMaharashtraHistoric west-coast trading centre.
ChaulMaharashtraKonkan coastal port connected with maritime merchants.
BharuchGujaratImportant trading centre in the historical Lata region.

These places should not all be treated as direct possessions of every Rashtrakuta king. Coastal control could vary, and local rulers or subordinate branches could exercise authority in particular areas. Their importance here is that the western coast connected the Rashtrakuta political world with overseas trade.

Horses were among the valuable commodities imported into India from western regions. Good cavalry horses were useful to rulers maintaining military forces. Commercial links therefore mattered not only for merchants and markets but also for the military resources available to kingdoms.

The specific Gujarat connection: Lata, Bharuch and Sanjan

Lata was a historical region broadly associated with southern Gujarat, including the area around Bharuch. A branch of the Rashtrakutas exercised authority in this region during parts of the early-medieval period.

This connection must be stated precisely. The existence of a Rashtrakuta branch in Lata does not mean that the imperial Rashtrakutas controlled the whole of present-day Gujarat throughout their history. Other dynasties also exercised power in different parts of Gujarat and neighbouring regions.

Bharuch was a major western Indian trading centre, while Sanjan, in present-day Valsad district, was another coastal settlement associated with early-medieval maritime commerce. Sanjan's location in modern Gujarat is worth remembering, even though historical accounts often discuss it together with ports of the wider northern Konkan and western coastal trading region.

Bringing the main Rashtrakuta facts together

The dynasty's history can be understood through 4 distinct associations. Dantidurga established independent power after overthrowing the Chalukyas. Krishna I is associated with the Kailasa temple, Cave 16, at Ellora. Amoghavarsha I is associated with the capital at Manyakheta and ruled when Sulaiman described the Balhara around 851 CE. Meanwhile, trade through ports such as Sanjan and Bharuch illustrates the connection between the Deccan and the western coast.

These associations concern different aspects of the same dynasty: political foundation, temple patronage, royal authority and commercial connections. Keeping them separate prevents the common mistake of assigning every achievement or place to the same ruler.

Prelims focus

  • Sulaiman: Arab merchant and writer whose account dates to around 851 CE.
  • Balhara: an Arabic rendering associated with the Rashtrakuta royal title Vallabharaja.
  • Amoghavarsha I: the Rashtrakuta ruler contemporary with Sulaiman's account.
  • Al-Masudi: Arabic writer of the early 10th century CE who described the Balhara and western coastal connections.
  • Gujarat connection: Lata in southern Gujarat, Bharuch and the port of Sanjan in present-day Valsad district.
  • Trap: Balhara was not a separate dynasty, and Sanjan is not located in present-day Maharashtra.

[IGNOU, History of India from c. 300 to 1206, BHIC-132, Unit 10, Emergence of Rashtrakutas, printed pp. 158–160, 2019; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Vol. I, Part I, History of Gujarat, Appendix V, Arab References, section c19.2 and related descriptions of the Balhara; An Emergent Coastal Polity: The Konkan Coast under the Silaharas, discussion of Arabic accounts and western coastal ports, consulted 18 November 2026; Kurush Dalal, In Pursuit of the Parsis: Early Medieval Entrepôt Sanjan, IGNCA online lecture abstract, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of Gujarat, Valsad district, History, consulted 18 November 2026.]
